questions.q: How do locking, blocking, and deadlocks relate to each other, per this lesson?
options: Locking is the mechanism that protects data; blocking is one session waiting on a lock (locking becoming a visible wait); a deadlock is circular blocking that SQL Server must resolve by killing a session
They are three interchangeable names for the exact same thing with no meaningful difference
Locking only happens during backups, never during normal queries
Blocking always means a deadlock has occurred
questions.explain: Locking is always happening and mostly healthy; blocking is expected under concurrency; a deadlock is the one case SQL Server can't resolve without killing a session.

questions.q: What does a row with request_status = 'WAIT' in sys.dm_tran_locks tell you?
options: That session is actively blocked right now, waiting for a lock another session is holding
That lock has already been released
The database is in single-user mode
A deadlock has just occurred
questions.explain: A GRANT status means the lock is held successfully; WAIT means the session is blocked waiting for it.

questions.q: How do you find the actual root-cause session in a blocking chain using sys.dm_exec_requests?
options: Chase blocking_session_id back through the chain until you reach the session whose own blocking_session_id is 0 -- that session isn't being blocked by anyone else
The root cause is always the session with the highest session_id number
It's impossible to determine the root cause of a blocking chain
The root cause is always the most recently started session
questions.explain: That session -- not blocked by anyone -- is the one actually holding up the rest of the chain, often due to a long-running uncommitted transaction.

questions.q: What makes a deadlock different from ordinary blocking?
options: A deadlock is specifically circular -- two sessions each wait on a lock the other holds, so neither can ever proceed, forcing SQL Server to kill one
A deadlock is just blocking that lasts longer than 30 seconds
A deadlock only happens on Azure SQL Managed Instance, never elsewhere
A deadlock means the database has run out of disk space
questions.explain: Ordinary blocking resolves itself once the blocking session finishes; a deadlock never resolves on its own because it's a cycle.

questions.q: What should application code do when it receives error 1205 (deadlock victim)?
options: Expect and retry the transaction, since being chosen as the deadlock victim is a normal, anticipated outcome of concurrency, not a fatal failure
Immediately shut down the entire application
Ignore the error completely and continue as if nothing happened
Manually restart the SQL Server service
questions.explain: SET DEADLOCK_PRIORITY LOW can influence which session is more likely to be chosen as the victim, but any session touching shared data should be written to retry on 1205.
